a OurBigBook.com
For the sawtooth Ising chain, there is a source inconsistency: the printed Ising spin values are {−1,r+1}, with no definition of r. The requested transfer matrix follows for r=0, namely the usual Ising model with values {−1,+1}. For arbitrary r, summing an apex spin actually gives
Ass′(r)​=e−βJss′[eβJˉ(s+s′)+e−βJˉ(r+1)(s+s′)].
(1)
For example, r=1, s=s′=−1 and βJˉ=1 give the bracket e−2+e4, whereas the claimed hyperbolic cosine gives e−2+e2. Thus the printed identity is false literally. The rest of Question 1 uses the intended symmetric Ising spin values, r=0.
For a fixed configuration of base spins, each apex spin appears in only one local Boltzmann factor. The apex spins are therefore conditionally independent, and their finite sums factorize:
Z​=s0​,…,sL−1​=±1∑​i=0∏L−1​[e−βJsi​si+1​sˉi​=±1∑​e−βJˉsˉi​(si​+si+1​)]=s0​,…,sL−1​=±1∑​i∏​Asi​si+1​​,sL​=s0​,Ass′​=2e−βJss′cosh[βJˉ(s+s′)],Z=TrAL.​​
(2)
Only the base spins carry information from one triangle to the next. The apex spins have already been summed out, so no apex index remains in the transfer matrix; the final trace implements the periodic boundary condition.

A=(ab​ba​),a=2e−βJcosh(2βJˉ),b=2eβJ,λ±​=a±b.
(3)
For finite positive temperature, a,b>0 and λ+​>∣λ−​∣. Consequently Z=λ+L​+λ−L​ and L−1logZ→logλ+​ in the thermodynamic limit. There are 2L spins, so the Helmholtz free energy per spin is
f(β,J,Jˉ)=−2β1​log[2e−βJcosh(2βJˉ)+2eβJ].​
(4)
The factor 1/2 is essential: one transfer matrix step counts two spins. For completeness, if the undefined r is retained, set ar​=A−1,−1(r)​, dr​=Ar+1,r+1(r)​ and br​=A−1,r+1(r)​. The same thermodynamic limit gives fr​=−(2β)−1log[(ar​+dr​+(ar​−dr​)2+4br2​​)/2] whenever these are two distinct spin values.

Differentiate the Helmholtz free energy at fixed couplings. With λ=λ+​ from solution, the entropy per spin is
s=−∂T∂f​=2kB​​(logλ−β∂β∂logλ​).
(5)
It is particularly useful to write
λ=eβ(2Jˉ−J)+e−β(2Jˉ+J)+2eβJ.
(6)
At Jˉ=J, this is 3eβJ+e−3βJ, so f=−J/2−(log3)/(2β)+o(β−1). For fixed Jˉ>J, the first exponential dominates alone, giving f=(J−2Jˉ)/2+o(β−1). Hence the residual entropy is
T→0lim​s={(kB​/2)log3,0,​Jˉ=J,Jˉ>J.​​
(7)
The finite positive difference Jˉ−J must be kept fixed in the second limit; taking it to zero first gives the other answer.
At high temperature, λ→4 and β∂β​logλ→0, whence
T→∞lim​s=kB​log2.​
(8)
All 22L configurations become equally probable because their Boltzmann factors tend to one. The two available states per spin, rather than the coupling values, determine this entropy.

d OurBigBook.com
For one triangle, equal base spins s=s′=σ give energy J+2Jˉσsˉ. Their minimum occurs at sˉ=−σ and is J−2Jˉ. Opposite base spins give energy −J, independently of the apex spin. The all-equal configurations have energy J+2Jˉ.
When Jˉ=J, the six configurations with precisely one spin different from the other two all have minimum energy −J. For a fixed first base spin, there is one minimum choice if the next base spin is the same, and two choices of apex if it is opposite. The ground-configuration counting transfer matrix is therefore
C=(12​21​),ΩL​=TrCL=3L+(−1)L.
(9)
This ground-state counting of the frustrated sawtooth Ising chain proves the extensive geometric frustration and the residual entropy kB​limL→∞​logΩL​/(2L)=(kB​/2)log3.
When Jˉ>J, J−2Jˉ<−J. Every triangle must have equal base spins and the opposite apex spin. Shared base spins propagate that choice around the chain, leaving just two global ground states, of energy L(J−2Jˉ). Their entropy per spin is kB​log2/(2L)→0.
For couplings favoring ferromagnetism, write J=−K, Jˉ=−Kˉ with K,Kˉ>0. Both orientations of an all-equal triangle minimize every bond simultaneously. The common base spins then make the whole chain uniform. There are two global ground states for either K=Kˉ or K=Kˉ, so no corresponding distinction in residual entropy occurs. This statement assumes all bonds remain nonzero.

a OurBigBook.com
The continuous internal symmetry is a common rotation around z:
Sj±​⟼e±iθSj±​,Sjz​⟼Sjz​.
(10)
Both the transverse exchange and the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction contain one raising and one lowering spin operator, so the phases cancel. Equivalently, [H,∑j​Sjz​]=0 and the continuous group is U(1).
The discrete internal symmetry is time reversal, TSj​T−1=−Sj​, together with TiT−1=−i. Each term in H contains two spin operators, so it is invariant. The operation is antiunitary; treating the reversal of all three spin components as a unitary rotation would violate the spin commutation relations. It reverses the magnetization and interchanges the two easy-axis ordered orientations. A convenient equivalent representative, composed with a z rotation, is Rz​(π)T, which reverses Sz while preserving Sx,Sy as operators.
The statement about one continuous and one discrete internal symmetry describes generic parameters. At D=0, additional unitary π rotations about transverse axes are allowed; at D=u=0, the continuous internal symmetry enlarges to full spin rotation symmetry. Spatial translations of the uniform chain are separate symmetries of the sites.

Solution

Words: 166
b OurBigBook.com
The Holstein–Primakoff transformation maps the finite spin basis ∣S,m⟩ to bosonic Fock states ∣n⟩ with n=S−m. Thus n=0 is the fully polarized reference state, and creating a boson lowers Sz by one. The physical subspace has the Holstein–Primakoff occupation constraint 0≤n≤2S, not the whole infinite oscillator Hilbert space.
The specified ordering of the square root gives
S+∣n⟩=n(2S−n+1)​∣n−1⟩,S−∣n⟩=(n+1)(2S−n)​∣n+1⟩.
(11)
These are the exact spin ladder operator matrix elements; in particular, the lowering amplitude vanishes at n=2S. The underlying oscillator obeys its usual canonical commutation relation on the enlarged space, while the spin operators preserve the constrained physical subspace. Projecting the oscillator operators themselves to a finite space would change their commutator at its upper endpoint.
Expanding 2S−n​=2S​(1−n/(4S)+⋯) converts an ordered spin problem to approximately free magnons, with interactions in higher orders of 1/S. Two complications are the nonpolynomial, order-sensitive square roots, which generate interacting bosons, and loss of the occupation bound when a truncated expansion uses the full bosonic Fock space. Large depletion, high temperature, or soft modes near a phase transition can invalidate the assumption ⟨n⟩≪S even when S is large.

−J(1+u)∑j​(S−nj​)(S−nj+1​)=−LJ(1+u)S2+2JS(1+u)∑j​nj​+O(S0).

Use
Sjx​Sj+1x​+Sjy​Sj+1y​(Sj​×Sj+1​)z​​=21​(Sj+​Sj+1−​+Sj−​Sj+1+​),=2i​(Sj+​Sj+1−​−Sj−​Sj+1+​).​

HLSW​=j∑​[Aaj+1†​aj​+A∗aj†​aj+1​+Bnj​],A=−S(J+iD),B=2JS(1+u).​

Choose the unitary discrete Fourier transform
aj​=L​1​∑k​eikjbk​,bk​=L​1​∑j​e−ikjaj​,k=L2πℓ​,ℓ=0,…,L−1.
(15)
The finite-sum orthogonality identity gives [bk​,bq†​]=δkq​. It also gives ∑j​aj+1†​aj​=∑k​e−ikbk†​bk​. Substituting A,B from solution therefore gives the dispersion relation
HLSW​=k∑​ϵ(k)bk†​bk​,ϵ(k)=2S[J(1+u)−Jcosk−Dsink].​
(16)
Using the opposite sign in the Fourier transform reverses k and the sine term together, without changing the spectrum.
For u≫1 every ϵ(k)>0, so the ground state of this quadratic Hamiltonian is the bosonic vacuum, bk​∣GS⟩=0 for every k. In the original spin variables it is the fully +z polarized product state. Its energy is zero after the constant subtraction. Repeating the construction about the fully −z polarized state describes the other easy-axis sector of the original Hamiltonian.
A one-magnon excitation bk†​∣GS⟩ has energy ϵ(k) above the reference ground state. A normalized many-magnon Fock state with occupations nk​ has excitation energy ∑k​nk​ϵ(k), within the dilute regime of the linear spin-wave approximation. The lowest excitation in this sector has the minimum allowed ϵ(k).

Let R=J2+D2​ and k0​=arctan(D/J). Since Jcosk+Dsink=Rcos(k−k0​), the continuum minimum of the dispersion relation is
Δ=2S[J(1+u)−R],uc​=1+(D/J)2​−1.​
(17)
For D>0, the energy gap closes at a positive uc​, at wave vector k0​. Below it, the quadratic expansion about the polarized state has a negative mode and is no longer a stable ground state approximation; higher-order terms and a different ordered reference state are needed.
Two qualifications are required by the actual assumptions. First, D=0 is permitted, in which case uc​=0; it is a concrete counterexample to the printed strict inequality uc​>0. Second, a finite ring only has discrete momenta. Its finite-ring spin-wave threshold with antisymmetric exchange is
uc​(L)=ℓ=0,…,L−1max​[cosL2πℓ​+JD​sinL2πℓ​]−1.​
(18)
This approaches uc​ in the thermodynamic limit and equals it when k0​ is allowed. For example, L=4 and 0<D<J give uc​(L)=0, since the maximum of 1,D/J,−1,−D/J is one. Thus the continuum formula and its positive threshold require the large-ring interpretation. The two symmetry-related polarized ground states already have equal exact energy; the calculated energy gap refers to excitations about one chosen orientation.

Here pn​(t) is the probability of occupying state n, and Wnm​ for n=m is the transition rate from m to n. More precisely, over dt>0 that transition has probability Wnm​dt+o(dt). This is a time-homogeneous continuous-time Markov chain: the present state contains all information needed for the next transition, the rates do not depend on time, and finite rates make multiple jumps have probability o(dt). In a physical rate description, untracked coherent dynamics or memory must be negligible on the timescale being modeled.
The master equation separates incoming and outgoing terms:
p˙​n​=∑m=n​(Wnm​pm​−Wmn​pn​),Wnm​≥0 (n=m),Wmm​=−n=m∑​Wnm​.​
(19)
Columns, rather than rows, sum to zero with this indexing. These conditions preserve normalization and nonnegative probabilities. For infinitely many states one also needs a well-defined nonexplosive process. Detailed balance is an additional equilibrium condition, not a general requirement on a master equation.

Write the probability column vector as p=(p0​,pA​,pB​)T, with 0 denoting the uncharged state. The arrows in the original figure give transitions 0→A at rate f1​, A→B at rate f2​, B→0 at rate f3​, and B→A at rate f4​. Exclusion of double occupation means injection occurs only from state 0. Thus the master equation is
dtd​​p0​pA​pB​​​=​−f1​f1​0​0−f2​f2​​f3​f4​−(f3​+f4​)​​​p0​pA​pB​​​.​
(20)
For example, p˙​B​=f2​pA​−(f3​+f4​)pB​. Every allowed jump adds to one probability and subtracts from another, which verifies the zero column sums.

Set the time derivatives in the master equation to zero. The first and third rows give f1​p0​=f3​pB​ and f2​pA​=(f3​+f4​)pB​. Normalization then gives, with N=f2​f3​+f1​(f3​+f4​)+f1​f2​,
p0st​=Nf2​f3​​,pAst​=Nf1​(f3​+f4​)​,pBst​=Nf1​f2​​.​
(21)
These expressions assume positive rates, or a limiting choice for which N=0 and the stationary distribution is unique. If rates vanish so that multiple closed classes appear, the initial condition can matter.
The word “equilibrium” in this part must mean a stationary distribution. With positive f1​,f2​,f3​ the one-way contact transitions support a nonzero stationary electric current, so the process is not in thermodynamic equilibrium and does not satisfy detailed balance. In particular, 0→A carries positive probability flow while the direct reverse rate is zero.

Count net transmitted charges per unit time, taking left-to-right as positive. The contact on the left, the internal bond, and the contact on the right give respectively
IL​=f1​p0st​,IAB​=f2​pAst​−f4​pBst​,IR​=f3​pBst​.
(22)
The backward rate f4​ must be subtracted in the internal count. Substitution of solution yields
IL​=IAB​=IR​=Nf1​f2​f3​​.​
(23)
The equalities also follow directly from p˙​0​=IR​−IL​=0 and p˙​B​=IAB​−IR​=0: there can be no stationary accumulation of electric charge. If each carrier has charge q, the electric current is qIR​. During a stationary interval of duration t, the expected net number crossing any one bond is IR​t. In particular, counting both directions of internal hopping as positive would count traffic, not transmitted charge.

y′=−y+2pB​,pA′​=y−pA​+pB​,pB′​=pA​−3pB​.

y′′+5y′+6y=2.

y=31​+Ce−2τ+De−3τ,C+D=−31​,−2C−3D=2,

whence
p(t)=31​+e−2ft−34​e−3ft.​

The free complex Proca field has Poincaré symmetry, with Bμ​ transforming as a spacetime four-vector, and the global internal U(1) symmetry
Bμ​⟼eiαBμ​,Bμ∗​⟼e−iαBμ∗​.
(28)
The free theory is also invariant under charge conjugation Bμ​↔Bμ∗​ and the usual parity and time reversal transformations of a vector field. The internal real-field description consists of two equal-mass real Proca fields, with an O(2) symmetry containing the phase rotations and charge conjugation.
A gradient shift of Bμ​ leaves Gμν​ unchanged, because partial derivatives commute. It changes the mass term by
ΔL=M2[−Bμ∗​∂μλ−(∂μ​λ∗)Bμ+(∂μ​λ∗)∂μλ].
(29)
This is generally nonzero: for example, Bμ​=0 and real λ=at produce ΔL=M2a2. Thus a massive Proca field has no such gauge symmetry. The massless kinetic term alone would have it.

Treat Bμ​ and Bμ∗​ as independent variables in the Euler-Lagrange equation. Varying Bν∗​ gives the Proca equation
∂μ​Gμν+M2Bν=0.
(30)
The divergence of its first term vanishes by antisymmetry and commuting partial derivatives. Since M=0, it follows that ∂ν​Bν=0. Substitution into the original equation gives
(□+M2)Bν=0,∂ν​Bν=0.​
(31)
The complex-conjugate variation gives ∂μ​G∗μν+M2B∗ν=0, hence (□+M2)B∗ν=0 and ∂ν​B∗ν=0.
For an on-shell plane wave Bμ=εμe−ipx, the Lorenz constraint in Proca theory is pμ​εμ=0. In the rest frame it sets ε0=0, leaving three complex particle polarizations. Thus the complex Proca field has three independent complex dynamical components, or six real ones; its quantized particle and antiparticle each have three physical particle polarizations. The conjugate field is not another unrelated classical field.

πμ​=−G∗0μ​,πμ∗​=−G0μ​,π0​=π0∗​=0.​

In particular, πi​=G∗0i and πi∗​=G0i. No time derivative of B0 appears, so the zero momenta are primary constraints, not invertible equations for B˙0.
For spatial indices, G0i=B˙i+∂i​B0​, so B˙i=πi∗​+∂iB0​, with the conjugate relation for B∗i. Also
L=∑i​∣G0i∣2−21​Gik∗​Gik+M2∣B0​∣2−M2∑i​∣Bi∣2.

The Legendre transform for the complex Proca Hamiltonian, Hc​=πi​B˙i+πi∗​B˙∗i−L therefore gives
Hc​=∫d3x[πi∗​πi​+πi​∂iB0​+πi∗​∂iB0∗​+21​Gik∗​Gik−M2B0∗​B0​−M2Bi∗​Bi].​

Repeated spatial indices in the positive product πi∗​πi​ denote an ordinary three-component sum. A total Hamiltonian additionally includes multipliers for π0​=π0∗​=0.
The Hamiltonian printed in the source cannot follow from the given complex Lagrangian density: its missing conjugations, mass coefficients and spatial mass sign are inconsistent. A concrete check is spatially uniform initial data B1=b∈R, B0=B2=B3=0, with all canonical momenta zero. The correct Hamiltonian density is M2b2, while the printed expression gives −M2b2/2. These data satisfy the initial constraints and evolve as a spatially uniform massive oscillator. Thus the discrepancy is not a harmless surface term or a different complex-field normalization.

0=π˙0​=−∂i​πi​+M2B0∗​,0=π˙0∗​=−∂i​πi∗​+M2B0​.

The naive equal-time canonical commutation relations would be
[Bμ(t,x),πν​(t,y)]=iδμν​δ(3)(x−y),[B∗μ(t,x),πν∗​(t,y)]=iδμν​δ(3)(x−y),
(38)
with all coordinate-coordinate, momentum-momentum and mixed conjugate-sector commutators zero before enforcing constraints. But the μ=ν=0 relation contradicts π0​=0 as an operator identity: its left side would vanish and its right side would not.
The primary zero-momentum constraints and the secondary massive Gauss laws form second-class constraints; their Poisson bracket matrix contains nonzero terms proportional to M2. They must be eliminated, or treated using a Dirac bracket, before quantization. In a reduced description the three complex spatial coordinates and their momenta are canonical, while
B0​=M2∂i​πi∗​​,B0∗​=M2∂i​πi​​
(39)
are dependent operators. Substituting them in the integrated Hamiltonian gives the positive density, up to a surface term,
Hred​=∑i​∣πi​∣2+M2∣∂i​πi​∣2​+21​Gik∗​Gik+M2∑i​∣Bi∣2.
(40)
Thus the problem is a constrained choice of canonical variables, not an absence of a consistent free quantum field theory.

Under Bμ′​=eiα(x)Bμ​ and Aμ′​=Aμ​−∂μ​Λ,
Dμ′​Bν′​=eiα[Dμ​Bν​+i(∂μ​α−e∂μ​Λ)Bν​].
(42)
Consequently the required relation is
∂μ​α=e∂μ​Λ,α=eΛ+constant.​
(43)
Then Gμν′​=eiαGμν​, its complex conjugate transforms oppositely, the mass bilinear is invariant, and Fμν′​=Fμν​. Each term in the total Lagrangian density is therefore invariant under the electromagnetic U(1) gauge symmetry. This phase gauge symmetry does not reinstate the broken gradient-shift gauge symmetry of the massive field itself.

Set Cμν​=Aμ​Bν​−Aν​Bμ​, so G=G+ieC. Expanding the minimally coupled Lagrangian density gives
Lint​=2ie​(Cμν∗​Gμν−Gμν∗​Cμν)−2e2​Cμν∗​Cμν.
(44)
Thus there is a derivative cubic ABB∗ interaction vertex of order e, and a quartic AABB∗ interaction vertex of order e2. There is no pure B4 contact term in this minimal coupling theory, nor an Abelian three-photon interaction vertex.
The straight arrowed lines in the original schematic denote charged massive vector bosons; the wavy lines denote photons. For two identical positively charged vector bosons, the leading scattering amplitude has the order-e2 t-channel photon-exchange Feynman diagram, together with its u-channel interchange required by identical bosons. A quartic AABB∗ interaction vertex cannot directly attach four external massive vector bosons. For a particle-antiparticle incoming pair, the leading channels instead are t-channel exchange and s-channel photon annihilation. The shown arrows track charge flow; an outgoing charged particle corresponds to the conjugate field at a vertex.

Putting F=Q, G=ϕa​(x) in the Poisson bracket definition therefore gives

Q=−ϵkPk​,Pk​=∫d3yπb​(y)∂k​ϕb​(y).
(47)
Since δQ/δπa​=−ϵk∂k​ϕa​, solution and antisymmetry of the Poisson bracket give
δˉϕa​={ϕa​,Q}PB​.​
(48)
Canonical quantization replaces the Poisson bracket by a commutator divided by iℏ:
δˉϕ^​a​=iℏ1​[ϕ^​a​,Q^​].​
(49)
With this sign convention one may use U=e−iQ^​/ℏ and ϕ^​a′​=U†ϕ^​a​U. Because Q=−ϵkPk​, the negative shift of the field argument follows with the required sign.

δπa​δH​=va​+(πb​−∂vb​∂L​)∂πa​∂vb​​=va​.

It follows that
{ϕa​,Q}PB​=δπa​δQ​=−ϵ0ϕ˙​a​=δˉϕa​.​

Tρμ​=∂(∂ρ​ϕa​)∂L​∂μ​ϕa​−δρμ​L.

Direct differentiation gives
∂ρ​Tρμ​=[∂ρ​∂(∂ρ​ϕa​)∂L​−∂ϕa​∂L​]∂μ​ϕa​=0

on solutions of the Euler-Lagrange equations. The four Noether currents are the four columns of this tensor, whereas their spatial integrals are the conserved four-momentum components:

For μ=0 this is the Hamiltonian; for a spatial lower index it is Pk​=∫πa​∂k​ϕa​. Under the paper's passive-translation convention, the corresponding generator is Q=−ϵμPμ​. Conservation of the integrated quantities also uses the stated vanishing boundary flux.

For the spatial momenta, integration by parts gives
δπa​δPi​​=∂i​ϕa​,δϕa​δPi​​=−∂i​πa​.

Their Poisson bracket is therefore
{Pi​,Pj​}PB​​=∫d3x[−∂i​πa​∂j​ϕa​+∂i​ϕa​∂j​πa​]=∫d3xπa​(∂i​∂j​ϕa​−∂j​∂i​ϕa​)=0.​

For the mixed case, P0​=H and the spatial generator acts on both canonical fields by differentiation: {ϕa​,Pi​}=∂i​ϕa​, {πa​,Pi​}=∂i​πa​. Hence, for a translation-invariant local Hamiltonian density,
{H,Pi​}PB​=∫d3x∂i​H=0.

Finally {H,H}PB​=0 by antisymmetry. Together these prove
{Pμ​,Pν​}PB​=0.​

The proof requires commuting derivatives and no surviving boundary terms. It expresses the Abelian translation subgroup of Poincaré symmetry at the level of its canonical generators.

[ap​,aq†​]=(2π)32ωp​δ(3)(p−q),[a,a]=[a†,a†]=0.

For the free real scalar field, π=ϕ˙​ and
P0​=21​∫d3x[π2+(∇ϕ)2+m2ϕ2],Pi​=∫d3xπ∂i​ϕ.

Substitution of the Fourier expansion produces spatial Dirac delta functions. Terms with two annihilation operators or two creation operators cancel: in P0​ their coefficient is −ωp2​+p2+m2=0, and in Pi​ their integral is odd under p↦−p. The two mixed terms combine, with normal ordering removing the vacuum constant, to give
P^μ​=∫dΠp​pμ​ap†​ap​.​

In particular, Pi​ contains the lower component pi​=−pi​ in this Minkowski metric convention.
To check commutativity without manipulating a square of a Dirac delta function, define Nf​=∫dΠp​f(p)ap†​ap​. The oscillator algebra gives [Nf​,aq​]=−f(q)aq​ and [Nf​,aq†​]=f(q)aq†​. Thus [Nf​,aq†​aq​]=0 and [Nf​,Ng​]=0. Taking f=pμ​, g=pν​ proves

(62)
These identities hold on the usual dense domain of finite-particle states, or can first be proved in a finite box and then continued to the continuum.

a OurBigBook.com
The real scalar field action has spacetime translations and Lorentz invariance, together giving Poincaré symmetry. With a real scalar transformation law it also has parity and time reversal. A generic polynomial potential has no continuous internal symmetry. The additional field reversal ϕ↦−ϕ is a symmetry precisely when every nonzero odd-power coupling vanishes. The free massless special case also admits a constant shift of ϕ; generic interactions remove it.
In mass units, [∂μ​]=1 and the dimensionless action requires [L]=D. Normalizing the kinetic term fixes the classical mass dimension of the scalar field:
2+2[ϕ]=D,[ϕ]=2D−2​,[m]=1.
(63)
For each interaction, [λn​]+n[ϕ]=D, so
[λn​]=D−2n(D−2)​.​
(64)
These are classical or engineering scaling dimensions; quantum corrections can change the scaling of operators and couplings. The scale transformation prescribed later has field weight one, which equals this canonical weight only at D=4.

For invariance for arbitrary fields and all constant α, the fixed nonzero kinetic term requires D=4. Then the mass term requires m=0, and every nonzero coupling must have n=4. Hence

including the free choice λ4​=0. At D=4 the canonical mass dimension is [ϕ]=1 and [λn​]=4−n, so only the quartic interaction has a dimensionless coupling. A mass introduces a scale. This recovers the same result from solution.
The fixed field weight in the question matters: if it were replaced by the general canonical weight (D−2)/2, the kinetic term could be invariant in other dimensions, and a nonzero monomial interaction would require n=2D/(D−2) for D=2. g OurBigBook.com
For a free real scalar field in four spacetime dimensions, L=(∂ϕ)2/2−m2ϕ2/2 and π=ϕ˙​. Canonical quantization promotes these canonical fields to Hermitian operator-valued distributions with equal-time canonical commutation relations
[ϕ(t,x),π(t,y)]=iδ(3)(x−y),[ϕ(t,x),ϕ(t,y)]=[π(t,x),π(t,y)]=0.
(75)
Expand the solution of the Klein-Gordon equation into positive- and negative-frequency modes:
ϕ(x)=∫dΠk​[a(k)e−ikx+a†(k)eikx],dΠk​=(2π)32ωk​d3k​,ωk​=k2+m2​.
(76)
Hermiticity pairs the two coefficients as adjoints. The field commutators are equivalent to
[a(k),a†(q)]=(2π)32ωk​δ(3)(k−q),[a,a]=[a†,a†]=0.
(77)
For example, inserting the expansion in [ϕ,ϕ˙​] yields two equal Fourier integrals, each with coefficient i/2, and hence iδ(3). The vacuum obeys a(k)∣0⟩=0, and repeated creation operators generate the symmetric bosonic Fock space. Normal ordering of the quadratic Hamiltonian removes its vacuum constant and gives H=∫dΠk​ωk​a†a; the same computation for the spatial momentum gives the stipulated four-momentum Pμ=∫dΠk​kμa†a.
The oscillator algebra now implies
[Pμ,a(k)]=−kμa(k),[Pμ,a†(k)]=kμa†(k).
(78)
Consequently
[Pμ,ϕ(x)]​=∫dΠk​[−kμa(k)e−ikx+kμa†(k)eikx]=−i∂μϕ(x)​.​
(79)
Indeed, ∂μe∓ikx=∓ikμe∓ikx. For μ=0, the result is [H,ϕ]=−iϕ˙​, which is the Heisenberg equation of motion with the correct sign. As usual, the field identities are interpreted after smearing the operator-valued distributions, or on a suitable common finite-particle domain.
